Air stripping pre-treatment process to enhance biogas production in 
anaerobic digestion of chicken manure wastewater 
Krailak Fakkaew a,*, Chongrak Polprasert b 
a Environmental Health Program, School of Health Science, Mae Fah Luang University, Thailand 
b Department of Civil Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, Thammasat University, Thailand   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Air stripping 
Chicken manure 
Anaerobic digestion 
Biogas production 
Ammonia 
A B S T R A C T   
Anaerobic digestion is typically applied for water and air pollution control and energy recovery from chicken 
manure wastewater. Unfortunately, high nitrogen content of the chicken manure could be prohibitive to efficient 
anaerobic digestion. In this study, air stripping was employed as a pre-treatment process for ammonia removal 
from a chicken manure wastewater. Laboratory-scale experiments of air striping were conducted at various 
temperatures, initial pH values, air flow rates, and stripping times. The experimental results showed that the high 
ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 80% could be achieved from the air stripping process operating at the 
initial pH, temperature, and air flow rate of 11, 80 ◦C, and 4.0 L/min, respectively. The ammonia removal ki­
netics were found to fit with the first-order reaction. Bio-methane potential tests suggested that air stripping pre- 
treatment of the chicken manure wastewater resulted in about 25% increase in biogas production.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a cost-effective and environmentally- 
friendly method which can treat and recover bio-energy from various 
types of organic wastes. AD of livestock wastes such as chicken and 
swine manures could yield considerable environmental and economic 
benefits, including water and air pollution control, and renewable en­
ergy production (Blumenstein et al., 2016; Cowley and Brorsen, 2018; 
Scarlat et al., 2018). Although chicken manure is rich in organic matters 
and has higher potentials for biogas production than swine and cow 
manures (Owamah et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2011), its high nitrogen 
content could be prohibitive to efficient anaerobic digestion. During 
microbial degradation, organic nitrogen is converted to ammonia which 
could act as a strong inhibitor on microbiological conversion in the AD 
process (Angelidaki and Ahring, 1993; Nielsen and Angelidaki, 2008). 
Total ammonia nitrogen concentration greater than 3 g/L could result in 
a decreased methane production (Bi et al., 2020; Calli et al., 2005; Chen 
et al., 2008; Yenigün and Demirel, 2013). To overcome the ammonia 
inhibition of AD, various ammonia reduction techniques have been 
developed including: substrate dilution, co-digestion with high‑carbon 
substrates, pH and temperature setting, use of additives with adsorptive 
capacity such as activated carbon, bentonite and zeolite, use of trace 
elements 
such 
as 
selenium, 
microflora

and 
bioaugmentation, stripping, membrane processes, struvite precipitation, 
ultrasonication and microwave irradiation, and biological process such 
as Anammox (Fuchs et al., 2018). 
Ammonia stripping is considered to be a cost-effective technique that 
requires relatively low energy inputs in which free ammonia is trans­
ferred from the wastewater into the gas phase (Li et al., 2018). Ammonia 
stripping experiments have been carried out by using a variety of 
techniques at different operating conditions such as pH, temperatures, 
and stripping agents (air, nitrogen, steam, or biogas) (Bonmati and 
Flotats, 2003; Georgiou et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 
2013; Ledda et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018; Nie et al., 2015; Serna-Maza 
et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2006). Successful applica­
tions of ammonia stripping have been reported both as a pre-AD process 
to various feedstocks, such as: domestic and industrial wastewaters, 
piggery and poultry wastes (Georgiou et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Li 
et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012), and as a post-AD process to the effluent 
of anaerobic digestion and digested dairy manure supernatant (Huang 
et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2007; Serna-Maza et al., 2015). 
Currently, ammonia stripping methods are based on pH and/or 
temperature of substrate. Because pH directly affects the distribution of 
ammonia forms (NH4
+/NH3) in aqueous solutions, raising pH to more 
than 11 results in the conversion of almost all the ammonium ions (NH4
+) 
into dissolved ammonia gases (NH3) (Tchobanoglous et al., 2003).

Substrate pH has higher effect on NH3 formation than temperature 
(Markou, 2015), but increasing pH can negatively influence the meth­
anogenesis causing lower biogas production (Chen et al., 2008). 
Therefore, optimum conditions among pH, temperature and air flow 
rate for air stripping of ammonia should be investigated, especially 
when a cheap energy source is available. 
The foremost objective of this study was to enhance biogas produc­
tion from the AD of chicken manure wastewater by ammonia removal 
using air stripping as a pre-AD process. The specific objectives were: (1) 
to determine optimum conditions for ammonia removal by air stripping, 
including determination of reaction rate constants and design criteria, 
and (2) to determine the efficiency of biogas production from the AD 
using air stripping as a pre-AD process. 
2. Methodology 
2.1. Materials 
Chicken manure wastewater samples were collected from a chicken 
farm located in Mae Chan District, Chiang Rai, northern Thailand. The 
main characteristics of the chicken manure wastewater are shown in 
Table 1. Digested sludge collected from the anaerobic lagoon of the 
Jampa farm wastewater treatment plant (Chiang Rai, Thailand) was 
used as an inoculum for bio-methane potential (BMP) test. 
2.2. Air Stripping experiments 
Air stripping experiments were conducted with a 1-L Duran glass 
bottle in a water bath (WNE22, Memmert, Germany) equipped with an 
aerator (ACO-9905, Hailea, China) and gas absorber, as illustrated in 
Fig. 1. The water bath was used to adjust temperatures of the experi­
ments. The gas absorber containing 5 M H2SO4 solution was used to 
absorb the stripped ammonia gas to prevent releasing of harmful gas to 
the environment. Each experiment was performed with 600 mL of 
chicken manure wastewater sample, and the operating conditions were 
controlled at the initial pH values of 7, 9 and 11; temperatures of 30, 50, 
70, 80, and 90 ◦C; and air flow rates of 0.5 and 4.0 L/min. The waste­
water samples were taken for analysis of the remaining ammonia con­
centrations at various stripping times. 
2.3. Bio-methane potential (BMP) Test 
BMP tests of the chicken manure samples, with and without air 
stripping pre-treatment, were conducted in triplicate using 1 L lab-scale 
anaerobic digesters. Each testing digester was filled with 400 mL of the 
mixture of chicken manure sample and inoculum at the substrate/ 
inoculum ratio of 0.5 gVS/gVS (Esposito et al., 2012). To create an 
anaerobic condition, all digesters were then filled with sufficient nitro­
gen gas to purge oxygen gas. Blank digesters, filled with 400 mL of the 
inoculum alone, were operated in parallel for data comparison. The BMP 
tests were carried out in a shaking water bath (WNE45, Memmert, 
Germany) controlled at the temperature of 37 ◦C, for 30 days. The 
produced biogas samples obtained from the BMP tests were collected 
and analyzed for their quantity and composition.

2.4. Analytical methods 
Characteristics of the chicken manure samples such as chemical ox­
ygen demand (COD), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5), total solids 
(TS) and total volatile solids (TVS) were determined according to the 
Standard Methods no. 5220-C, 5210-B, 2540-B and 2540-E, respectively 
(APHA, 2012). Total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN) and ammonia nitrogen 
(NH3−N) were measured using an automatic distillation unit machine 
(UDK149, VELP SCIENTIFICA, USA). Significant effects of the process 
parameters were statistically analyzed according to the response surface 
methodology (RSM) (Montgomery, 2005). Ammonia removal efficiency 
was calculated by using Eq. (1) as follows, 
E = (c0 −c)/c0 x 100
(1)  
where E is the ammonia removal efficiency (%), c0 and c are the initial 
and remaining NH3-N concentrations in the chicken manure wastewater 
(mg/L), respectively.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effects of pH, temperature and air flow rate 
Ammonia removal efficiencies obtained from the experiments at 
various air stripping conditions are shown in Fig. 2. A normal plot of the 
standardized effects (response is ammonia removal efficiency and α =
0.05) shown in Fig. 3 indicates that the initial pH, temperature and air 
flow rate had a significant effect on ammonia removal efficiency. The 
increases in the initial pH from 7 to 9 and 9 to 11 (Fig. 2A and B) caused 
the ammonia removal efficiencies to increase from 40 to 65% and from 
65 to 80%, respectively, probably because most of the ammonia nitro­
gen was transformed to become free ammonia gas (NH3), suitable for air 
stripping. At the pH levels above 9, the ammonia gas was predominant 
(Tchobanoglous et al., 2003). After completion of the air stripping 
process, due to the removal of free ammonia gas, the final pH values 
were decreased from 9 and 11 to about 8.5 and 9.7, respectively. 
Fig. 2A and C revealed that high ammonia removal efficiencies were 
obtained at the elevated wastewater temperatures. At higher tempera­
tures, the ammonia gas became more vapored and could be easier 
removed from the chicken manure samples with the supplied air. More 
than 60% and 80% of removal efficiencies were obtained at the

temperatures higher than 65 and 80 ◦C, respectively. Similarly, the 
higher air flow rates also resulted in higher ammonia removal effi­
ciencies in which more than 80% could be achieved at the air flow rate 
of 4.0 L/min. 
The interactions among the initial pH, temperatures and air flow 
rates on ammonia removal efficiencies are represented in Figs. 2 and 3. 
The interactions between air flow rate – temperature (Fig. 3, factor AB) 
and air flow rate – initial pH (Fig. 3, factor AC) had significant effects on 
ammonia removal efficiency. Statistical analysis results in Fig. 3 indi­
cated that the ammonia removal efficiency could be increased with 
increasing both air flow rate and temperature (or air flow rate and initial 
pH), simultaneously. 
At the neutral pH of 7, increasing the air flow rates did not have 
significant effects on the ammonia removal efficiency. Even at the air 
flow rate of 4.0 L/min, the ammonia removal efficiencies were not 
higher than 60% (Fig. 2). At the initial pH of 11, operating at temper­
atures and air flow rates of more than 80 ◦C and 2.2 L/min, respectively, 
resulted in ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 60%. 
At the lower temperatures (30 and 50 ◦C), increasing the air flow 
rates did not have significant effects on the ammonia removal effi­
ciencies, but increasing initial pH resulted in increased ammonia 
removal efficiencies. When the air stripping was operated at the tem­
perature of 90 ◦C, the ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 60% 
could be achieved at the operating air flow rates and initial pH of more 
than 2.8 L/min and 9, respectively. 
If operating the air stripping process at the low air flow rate of 0.5 L/ 
min, increasing both temperature and initial pH did not produce sig­
nificant effects on the ammonia removal efficiencies. However, at the 
higher air flow rate of 4.0 L/min, increasing the temperatures and initial 
pH to more than 85 ◦C and 9, respectively, resulted in increased 
ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 60%. 
The experimental results shown in Fig. 2 summarily indicated that 
the ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 80% could be achieved 
when the air stripping process was conducted at the initial pH, tem­
perature and air flow rate of 11, 80 ◦C, and 4.0 L/min, respectively. The 
response optimization analyzed by using RSM suggested the options of 
the air stripping conditions to achieve the ammonia removal efficiencies 
of more than 60%, as shown in Table 2. 
3.2. Kinetic models 
Because the ammonia removal efficiencies were influenced by the 
stripping temperatures, the ammonia removal kinetics were determined 
at various temperatures, as shown in Fig. 4. The obtained kinetic models 
and k values are listed in Table 3, with coefficients of determination (R2) 
being more than 0.90, which are comparable with those reported in the 
literatures. These experimental results indicated that ammonia removal 
reaction was a good fit for the first-order reaction, although some k 
values were different because of different stripping conditions employed 
in the previous studies (Serna-Maza et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2011). 
However, the k values obtained from this study should be applicable for 
the design and operation of the air stripping process for ammonia 
removal from chicken manure wastewater. 
Estimation of temperature effects on reaction rates using the 
Arrhenius equation is shown in Fig. 5, with the R2 value of 0.9545. The 
Ea and A values were found to be 18,150 J/mol and 1.232, respectively.

3.3. Biogas Production 
Although air is frequently employed as a strip gas in ammonia 
stripping process (Huang and Shang, 2006), oxygen contained in the air 
could act as a strong inhibitory agent to the anaerobic microorganisms 
such as acetogens and methanogens involved in the methane production 
(Whitman et al., 2006). From the results shown in Table 1, after the air 
stripping process, the COD, BOD5, TS and TVS concentrations were 
found to be slightly changed, but the NH3-N concentrations were 
significantly decreased while DO concentrations were increased. 
To evaluate the effects of the air stripping process on methane pro­
duction, the BMP tests were conducted. Fig. 6 shows the cumulative 
biogas production from the chicken manure with and without air 
stripping pre-treatment process during the 30 days operation. The 
chicken manure sample after the air stripping process exhibited slower 
biogas production, but eventually resulted in higher biogas yield than 
that without air stripping. The biogas yields of about 57.3 and 45.2 L per 
kg-VS were achieved from the AD of the chicken manure wastewater 
samples with and without air stripping pre-treatment, respectively. 
These results revealed that, probably due to less effects of ammonia 
inhibition (Table 1), the air stripping pre-treatment of the chicken 
manure resulted in about 25% increase in biogas production. 
4. Conclusions 
The experimental results of this study suggested that the air stripping 
conditions such as initial pH, temperature, and air flow rate had sig­
nificant effects on the ammonia removal efficiencies. To achieve the 
ammonia removal efficiency of 80%, the optimum operating conditions 
for the initial pH, temperature, and air flow rate were found to be 11, 
80 ◦C, and 4.0 L/min, respectively. The ammonia removal kinetics were 
found to fit with the first-order model. By using the air stripping process 
as a pre-treatment of the AD, the biogas production was found to in­
crease by about 25%.
